title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
hook: an empty clay pot holds a little piece of sky. Gaudapada asks what happens to that sky when the pot breaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika and the patience of steadying a mind, like emptying the ocean with a blade of grass. When your attention drifted, did you bring it back as calmly as the first time? Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: A BLADE OF GRASS AND THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: An empty clay pot sits on a kitchen shelf. Empty, we say. But it isn't quite empty. Inside it there is space, a small round piece of the same open space that fills the kitchen, the street, the sky over the house. Pour water in and the water takes up that space. Pour it out and the space is still there, shaped like the pot. Now drop the pot. It shatters on the floor. The clay is in pieces. Where did the space inside it go? It didn't fly anywhere. It didn't break. It just stopped looking separate. Gaudapada uses exactly this picture in the Mandukya Karika, and today we follow it.
screen: `AN EMPTY POT ON A SHELF.` → `A PIECE OF THE SAME SPACE.` → `THE POT BREAKS. WHERE DID IT GO?`

segments.voice: In the Karika's section called Advaita, not-two, Gaudapada says the self is like space. Living beings, each of us, are like the space inside pots. The pots seem to make many small spaces out of one. When the pots are broken, he says, the space in each one merges back into space. So it is with living beings and the self. Then he answers the obvious objection. If we're all one self, why does one person suffer while another is happy? His reply stays with the pots. If the space in one pot is filled with dust and smoke, the space in every other pot isn't dirty. So one person's joy or grief doesn't spill into all the others. Forms differ, uses differ, names differ, he says, yet space itself is not divided. Other Vedanta schools read the self and living beings as truly distinct, and they answer this image in their own way. Gaudapada adds a careful line. The space in the pot is not a piece cut out of space, and not something space turned into. In the same way, a living being is not a part of the self or a change in it. Last comes an image from childhood. To children, he says, the sky can look dirty. The dirt is in the seeing, not in the sky. In the same way, the self only seems stained to those who don't yet see clearly. The smoke drifts, the pot breaks, and the sky was never touched.
screen: `THE SELF IS LIKE SPACE.` · `SMOKE IN ONE POT, NOT IN ALL.` · `NOT A PIECE, NOT A CHANGE.` · `THE DIRT IS IN THE SEEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the space in the room. Sit, and let the breath slow down on its own. Look at a cup, a bowl, or a box near you, and notice the space inside it. Then the space around it. Then the room's space, running out through a window or a door. Close your eyes if you like, and rest in the sense of open space around the body. When a thought arrives, let it be like smoke in one pot. It doesn't change the space. If you pray, you can rest in that openness as an offering. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where the self is pictured as open space, and each life as space held for a while inside a pot. Today's word.

Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. Today, when you pour something out of a cup or a jar, pause on the space that's left. It was there before you filled it. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta often read the Mandukya Karika with Shankara's commentary under a teacher, and the image of space in a pot is still used in talks and classes to point to the self.

match.prompt: the pot and the space — tap the pairs.
pairs: a stain in the seeing, not the sky

myth: Gaudapada says one person's suffering fills everyone else's
smoke in one pot doesn't dirty the space in every pot. one person's grief stays their own.
the Karika says the space in a pot is not a piece cut out of space
not a part, not a change: and so, he says, with a living being and the self.
Gaudapada says the sky really is dirty, and only children notice
he says the sky looks dirty to children: the dirt is in the seeing, not in the sky.

fork.setup: a student asks Gaudapada: if we're all one self, why is one person sad while another is happy? you're Gaudapada. what do you say?
options: we aren't really one self at all.
smoke in one pot doesn't dirty the space in the others.
everyone is secretly feeling the same thing.
fork.reveal: he stays with the pots: the dust and smoke in one don't stain the rest, and space itself is never divided.

original.note: Sanskrit: the space in a pot, from ghata, a pot, and akasha, space. The Karika's word for the image.

trapdoor: what you thought: an empty pot is just empty.
what it means: for Gaudapada, the space inside it is the one space, only seeming separate, like a living being and the self.

what a scholar hears: Mandukya Karika 3.3–3.8, where the pot-space answers objections: one pot's smoke doesn't soil all, the pot-space is neither part nor modification of space, and children see the sky as dirty.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 3.3–3.8 (the self like space; living beings like the space in pots; when pots break the spaces merge; smoke in one pot does not soil all; names and forms differ but space does not; neither part nor modification; the sky looks dirty to children)
